# II. THE WATER TANK [italic]Entry two. Day 207. The pump room is warm and nobody comes down after midnight.[/italic]
I will not name the ship. She was old, she leaked air at the seams of the lower deck, and we loved her the way you love a dog that bites.
We were holding off a frontier world, close enough to see its lights. There were American ships in the same sky. Every watch the speakers said the standoff could become a war within the hour. Men slept in their armour. Two of us were caught writing letters home, and the letters were read aloud at muster.
The quartermaster had a business. Everyone knew. A colony hauler would come alongside in the shadow of the moon, and he would trade our spare rations and filters for medicine, cigarettes and real coffee. I was on his loading detail because I kept my mouth shut. It is the only skill the Union ever paid me for.
The last empty water tank on the pallet had a loose hatch. I looked at that hatch for three weeks. In the fourth week I climbed inside with a ration bar, a bottle of water and my identity disc, and pulled it shut.
Nineteen hours in the dark. I heard the clamps, the burn, the hauler crew arguing in English about cargo weight. I counted my heartbeats to ten thousand and started again. When the tank was opened, a woman with a torch looked at me for a long time. Then she threw me a coverall with someone else's name on it. She said nothing then. She has said nothing since.
On the ship they will have called it an accident. Lost in an airlock, maybe. Or they wrote the true word, [color=#C9442C]deserter[/color], and sent it to my mother's block, and the woman at the canteen punches her card a little harder now.
I do not know which. I think about it every time I eat.
